expected: Per app/institutions/parse.py's own module docstring and _resolve_nport_key's docstring, the key-resolution cascade exists specifically so a row 'this parser cannot cleanly identify... [is keyed] on the least-bad identifier available.' The CUSIP branch already guards against exactly this failure mode -- 'candidate != "N/A"' -- but the LEI branch two lines later has no equivalent guard, so a literal '<lei>N/A</lei>' (a real, common SEC convention for 'not applicable', not a genuine LEI) is accepted as if it were a real identifier, producing 'LEI:N/A' instead of falling through to the issuer name or, better, the filing's own <title> field which is populated for this exact row. A user reading 'Issuer: N/A' with a 'New' badge next to a $12M-$31M swing has no way to tell this is a CME equity-index future used for cash-equitization (routine for an index ETF) rather than an unidentified equity purchase.

GET /api/institutions/QQQ/changes confirms the wire values: cusip='LEI:N/A', issuer='N/A', action='new', value_after='-12012436.80000000'.

suggested_fix: In _resolve_nport_key, exclude the literal 'N/A' (case-insensitive) from the LEI branch the same way the CUSIP branch already does, and add a further fallback to <title> (then <identifiers><ticker>) before falling back to the bare issuer <name> -- title is populated on this exact row when name is not.
title: NPORT derivative row with literal LEI 'N/A' renders unidentifiable, ignoring the filing's own title/ticker

verification.note: Confirmed, and worse than reported. `_resolve_nport_key` tested the `N/A` sentinel on the CUSIP only; the ISIN and LEI branches checked emptiness alone. Reproduced against the live filing: QQQ's CME E-Mini NASDAQ 100 future has `<name>`, `<lei>` and `<cusip>` all equal to the literal string `N/A`, so it keyed on `LEI:N/A`, displayed an issuer called `N/A`, and carried -$12,012,436.80 badged NEW in the same styling as an equity purchase. ARK's OpenAI position hit the same branch at $177,028,452.35. The display was the lesser problem: `LEI:N/A` is a key two rows can share, so two unidentifiable rows in one filing would be grouped and summed into a single position that no filing reported. The rows are not actually anonymous -- that future carries `<title>CME E-Mini NASDAQ 100 Index Future</title>` and `<ticker value="NQM6"/>`, both of which the resolver was ignoring. Fixed: the sentinel is tested at every step, `<ticker>` joins the chain ahead of the LEI (an LEI names the counterparty, not the instrument), `<title>` supplies the issuer name when `<name>` is a sentinel, and a per-row ordinal is the terminal fallback so the key cannot collide by construction. Verified live: the row now reads `TICKER:NQM6` / `CME E-Mini NASDAQ 100 Index Future`, and every key in the filing is unique.

why_it_matters: Alex's whole reason for using this page is 'this institution just moved on something I hold or recognize' -- a professional reflex to walk every number back to what it actually is. A $12M position badged 'New' exactly like a real equity buy, with no name, no ticker and a nonsensical 'LEI:N/A' identifier, is a number I cannot act on or even correctly interpret without going to the raw XML myself, which defeats the point of the page. It also occurs on 2 of the 2 NPORT funds I checked (QQQ, IVV), so it is not a one-off -- any index ETF that holds index futures for cash management will show this on every filing pair.

title: Institutions counts strip and holdings total ignore active filters, staying unchanged when the table below is empty

verification.note: Confirmed by reading the render: `<CountsStrip counts={delta.counts} />` rendered the server's unfiltered tally directly above a table driven by the filtered `rows`. With a filter hiding everything, the strip announced NEW 566 / TRIM 1489 over 'No rows match the current filters'. Fixed: each tile shows `shown of total`, with a line stating how many positions are hidden, and the Full holdings table gained the same qualifier. The server's tally remains the authority for the total -- the client counts only what it actually renders, which is the one thing it is entitled to count. One correction to the first version of my own fix, caught by looking at the live page: it keyed on 'a checkbox is ticked' rather than 'rows are missing', so QQQ -- which has no `hold` rows at all -- read '95 of 95' beside 'Filters are active: 104 of 104'. A qualifier that fires when nothing is hidden teaches a reader to ignore it where it matters. It now keys on the count of hidden rows.

why_it_matters: This is the precise pattern the project has been bitten by before (see the persona brief's own warning about 'a count that describes the unfiltered set beside a table showing the filtered one'). A user who checks 'only holdings I also own' expecting to see what overlaps their book, sees a HOLD count of 6 and a total of 506 holdings sitting directly above an empty table with no explanation, and has no way to tell from the page alone whether the filter did nothing, whether the fund genuinely has 0 overlap, or whether something is broken -- exactly the ambiguity a professional needs resolved before trusting a page enough to route a real book through it.

verification.note: Confirmed -- the column had no `SortHeader`. Fixed, and the null case was handled deliberately rather than incidentally: `shares_pct_change` is `null` for a NEW position because there is no prior share count to divide by, so sorting it as zero would file the quarter's most decisive buys among the positions that did not move. New positions now sort together at the end in both directions.

why_it_matters: Ranking by relative size of a share-count change (not just absolute shares or dollar value) is a real, common question -- 'what did this manager do the most, proportionally' -- and this table has no way to answer it by sorting, only by scanning up to thousands of rows by eye.

expected: Two ordinary, simultaneous page-load requests to the thesis endpoints should not be able to produce an unhandled 500 from a WAL-mode-setup race; either the connection setup should tolerate a locked database with a short retry, or the two connections should not race on it at all.
observed: Navigating to /thesis/XLE fires GET /api/thesis/ledger?symbol=XLE and GET /api/thesis/holdout?symbol=XLE concurrently. In the backend log, /api/thesis/holdout returned 500 with the traceback: app/api/thesis.py:515 thesis_holdout -> app/thesis/holdout.py:135 load -> app/thesis/ledger.py:90 _connect -> conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL") -> sqlite3.OperationalError: database is locked. The very next request to the same endpoint, a moment later, returned 200 OK with no other change.
title: Thesis page's ledger and holdout requests can race on sqlite connection setup, producing an uncaught 500

verification.note: The mechanism is confirmed, the occurrence is not. `sqlite.connect` passes no `timeout` and sets no `busy_timeout` pragma, so it takes sqlite3's 5-second default; WAL lets readers and a writer coexist but still serialises two writers, so a concurrent write to the same ledger can surface as 'database is locked'. I did not reproduce the 500 -- the thesis holdout writes permanently to the ledger and re-running it to chase a race is not a cost worth paying here. Pre-existing and unrelated to this feature. Left open at the reported severity rather than upgraded on a mechanism I have not seen fire.

why_it_matters: This is the same class of defect as the already-fixed R2-5 (activity-import-panel-transient-500) -- a race that self-resolves on reload and could easily be mistaken for a flaky network blip rather than a reproducible concurrency bug, unless the backend log is read directly. The page itself did not visibly break (the frontend simply re-fetches), but a genuinely locked database under heavier concurrent load would surface as a real user-facing failure, not just a log line.

expected: compareDecimalStrings' own docstring commits to never parsing a DecimalString into a float for ordering, specifically to avoid a naive lexicographic or IEEE-double comparison mishandling a negative sign or precision beyond what a double preserves. observed: On QQQ's Changes table (104 rows), sorting 'Value Δ' ascending put Microsoft (-$8,238,972,123.60) first and the -$12,012,436.80 derivative row at position 70 of 104 -- correctly between larger negative swings and the smaller-magnitude ones, not string-sorted. Sorting 'Weight now' ascending produced a monotonically increasing sequence starting with the derivative row's -0.00003228571304700771... (rendered -0.00%), then two exact-zero EXIT rows (AstraZeneca, Ferrovial, both weight_after=0), then 0.06%, 0.09%, 0.11%... up to NVIDIA's 8.69% last.
title: POSITIVE: Changes table sorts negative and near-zero decimal values correctly, including the derivative row's weight

verification.note: Confirmed -- ordering is done on BigInt-scaled decimal strings, never parseFloat.

why_it_matters: This is exactly the failure mode the run brief called out as a real risk (a null sorting as zero, or a negative value sorting as if it were positive), and it is the kind of correctness that is easy to silently regress the next time this comparator is touched -- worth protecting.
